header:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-15 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Emily Soto (Lark Platform), Sam Gupta (Lark CTO), Daniel Kim (Lark SRE)
summary: Deep dive into KV cache behavior under interleaved long-context sessions. Discussed an unusual eviction pattern where prefixes are left as tombstones and cause paging churn during bursts. Compared hosted vs on-prem spill behaviors and outlined telemetry and repro steps.
transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — we want to walk through the eviction pattern you saw, dig into prefix tombstoning, and then talk about mitigations: prefetch heuristics, batching adjustments, and on-prem spill specifics.
[00:10] Sam: Yep, thanks. We've been seeing weird latency spikes every time multiple long-context sessions interleave, like when agents A and B alternate requests to the same conversation prefixes. It looks like the KV layer is thrashing.
[00:25] Marcus: Right, and to be clear, we saw eviction even though overall memory wasn't at 100%. There were these "stale prefixes" that seemed marked with a tombstone and when they were re-requested, the runtime paged them from NVMe causing a 400-800ms token penalty.
[00:40] Emily: And the weird bit is that some prefixes stayed stale for minutes, not seconds. We expected TTL-based eviction but this seems correlated with interleaving patterns rather than simple LRU.
[00:55] Priya: Mmh, okay. Two immediate hypotheses: one, the prefix hash collision and affinity causing eviction on sibling slabs; two, the tombstoning path in the KV implementation that marks keys but doesn't free underlying pages immediately to avoid concurrent readers.
[01:12] Daniel: Could be. We're on Redwood Private on prem, with HBM for active cache and NVMe for spill. We also have the runtime configured to keep a small reserve to avoid OOM during big prompts.
[01:28] Marcus: That reserve can interact badly with prefix reuse. If a hot prefix cycles between sessions that each hold different partial context, the runtime might choose to "tombstone" the older representation to avoid expensive merges, then reconstruct on demand — that reconstruct path is expensive.
[01:45] Sam: Are you saying it's a correctness decision for concurrency? Like to prevent a race you tombstone and then lazily reconstruct?
[01:51] Marcus: Exactly. It's an optimization for concurrency safety but can have poor perf under interleaved access patterns.
[02:05] Emily: We also noticed NVMe throughput spikes at the same time as the latency spikes. So it's consistent with spill/paging.
[02:12] Avery: Quick note — our hosted runtime uses different heuristics; we can switch to an alternative tombstone policy on private but it trades off memory fragmentation. We should show you the trade-offs with telemetry.
[02:30] Sam: Can you walk us through a timeline example — like, request A hits prefix p1 for 400 tokens, then request B hits p1 for 200 tokens, then A again?
[02:40] Marcus: Sure. In that scenario the runtime keeps two partial KV snapshots in HBM. To avoid duplicating too much, we tombstone older snapshots and keep a pointer. If a subsequent request needs the older logical view it triggers a reconstruction from spill, which is the expensive NVMe read.
[02:58] Emily: So the problem is the runtime's heuristic assumed temporal locality that our workload violates because we interleave long-running dialogs across many users.
[03:12] Priya: Exactly. The mitigation space: 1) aggressive prefix coalescing so both session deltas share a canonical snapshot; 2) change tombstone TTL to be shorter/longer depending on observed reuse windows; 3) prefetch heuristics that detect interleaving and warm the NVMe->HBM path proactively.
[03:34] Daniel: For prefetching, are we likely to overload NVMe with speculative reads? We've got a budget and don't want to spike costs.
[03:42] Marcus: It's tunable. We can set a conservative prefetch: only prefetch if a prefix has been accessed twice within X minutes by distinct sessions, or if the heatmap shows >Y qps.
[03:54] Sam: Okay. How about batching? Does larger token-level batching help or hurt this case?
[04:00] Marcus: Batching helps per-token throughput but hides latency for cold prefixes. If batch windows combine requests from different sessions, they may increase the chance of reusing cached KV, which is good. But if batching delays a request that would have reused a hot prefix, it can tip into eviction. So there's a sweet spot.
[04:20] Emily: Another variable: quantization. We're running an 8-bit quantized model to save memory. Does quantization affect KV sizes or spill frequency?
[04:28] Marcus: Quant itself doesn't change the KV shape, but lower precision reduces model working set size which can change eviction pressure. On some encoders the reduced working memory means KV cache stays resident more often, so it's overall beneficial, but it interacts with HBM fragmentation.
[04:45] Priya: Also for on-prem NVMe spill, the write amplification and asynchronous compaction can cause background IO that coincides with your bursts. We should look at NVMe SMART counters and compaction schedules.
[04:59] Daniel: We'll pull NVMe iostat and SMART logs.
[05:05] Sam: We also need SSO and KMS considerations — our security team mandates HSM-backed KMS and no unencrypted spill. Does Redwood support encrypted spill to NVMe?
[05:15] Avery: Yes, Private supports encrypted spill via your KMS/HSM. We can show the configuration we use: encrypted at rest for NVMe, and keys are pulled via customer KMS. There is a small CPU cost for decrypt on page-in but it's usually minimal compared to NVMe latency.
[05:32] Emily: Good. If decrypt adds 30ms that's acceptable compared to 400-800ms we saw.
[05:37] Marcus: Right. Another angle: prefix affinity and routing. If you can route related sessions to the same inference shard (node), you reduce cross-node spill and cold reads. That requires sticky routing/consistent hashing at your LB.
[05:53] Sam: We have a VPC-level router. Can Redwood provide a policy to pin conversation prefixes to a node?
[05:59] Priya: We can. There's a routing policy in Dedicated/Private to keep affinity on prefix hash. Trade-off: it can create hotspots on a node under skew. Our plan would be to combine affinity with token-budget-aware fallback so heavily skewed prefixes spill to a sibling node.
[06:17] Emily: Is there telemetry we can get to decide if affinity helps? Like per-prefix QPS and reuse window?
[06:22] Marcus: Yes — the KV telemetry dashboard shows per-prefix access frequency, hit ratio, last-access delta, and reconstruction count. We'll share that heatmap.
[06:31] Sam: Can you explain the "reconstruction count" metric?
[06:34] Marcus: It's number of times a tombstoned prefix had to be fully rebuilt from spill. Each reconstruction correlates strongly with the high-latency events you saw.
[06:44] Daniel: Is reconstruction single-threaded? We saw CPU cores spiking during rebuilds.
[06:49] Marcus: The default is serialized per-prefix to avoid concurrent writes, which risks higher latency. We can enable concurrent rebuilds with optimistic merging but that risks transient duplication and memory overhead.
[07:04] Avery: We'll propose a staged mitigation: short-term — increase tombstone TTL and enable conservative prefetch; mid-term — enable affinity for high-heat prefixes; long-term — provide an optimized concurrent-rebuild path and a more explicit API for prefix lifecycle.
[07:20] Priya: For the quick repro, Marcus — can you outline the script?
[07:24] Marcus: Yes — we simulate N sessions, each with long context (400-800 tokens) that touch overlapping prefixes every 30s, interleaving across sessions. We instrument to record reconstruction events, NVMe IO, and per-token latency. We can run it against your private cluster or a small dedicated pool.
[07:41] Emily: We'll run it Monday in our staging. Daniel will collect NVMe metrics.
[07:45] Daniel: Yep. We'll also attach traces with request ids.
[07:50] Sam: Any risk this changes behaviour in production if we flip TTL?
[07:54] Marcus: Changing TTL could increase resident memory and fragmentation; in worst case you'd need to add capacity. We'll quantify expected memory delta from historical access patterns before recommending a number.
[08:06] Avery: Also worth mentioning: model quantization profile. Some of our customers saw that switching from 8-bit to 4-bit reduced HBM enough to keep more KV resident and reduced reconstruction by ~18% for similar workloads. Not always applicable but we'll test.
[08:22] Emily: Okay. On compliance — can you share the on-prem spill encryption docs and SOC2 bits?
[08:28] Avery: Yes, we'll share the security pack after the call.
[08:31] Marcus: One last operational note — your scheduler shows spotty compaction windows overlapping your bursts. If we shift compaction windows to low-traffic periods you may see fewer NVMe IO collisions.
[08:45] Daniel: We can change compaction schedule.
[08:48] Priya: Great. Recap: Redwood will share KV heatmap and telemetry, Marcus will supply a repro script, Avery will share security docs, Lark will run synthetic interleaved session test and provide NVMe and trace logs.
[09:05] Sam: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:09] Avery: Thanks — we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the NVMe walkthrough and the repro results.
[09:14] [end of recording]
